correctness.rationale: Derived the complete frame spectrum by Fourier diagonalization and checked strict frame positivity. Proved root-sum squared-modulus gap product identity, strict log-cosine smoothing and exact second-best gap classification; proved the uniform rho2>4rho/3 via explicit trigonometric estimates and checked N=4,5,8 separately. A sampled-cosine lower bound then strictly excludes every unbalanced frequency triple even for the condition-number functional (not merely the root modulus). Direct cosine extrema establish the parity formulas, and trace-square Fourier orthogonality gives the exact potential defect. Complete brute-force enumeration N=4..40 and direct frame-operator checks N=4..11 pass; these are checks only, not the all-N proof. Quantifiers cover every N>=4, all generating shifts, all distinct triples.

originality.rationale: The 2026 full-translation diagonalization gives the spectrum, but no sharp optimization over three selected modulations. A fully inspected published three-row Riesz problem has the same almost-equilateral optimizer but a different 3-by-3 Gram operator, and the minimax gap/projection step does not follow from its theorem. Classical roots-of-unity sum minimization is explicitly not claimed as new. The proof supplies a sharp parity- and residue-class-dependent Gabor condition number, all equality sets, and potential defect. Unindexed older equivalent designs remain a risk.
residual_risks: The 1986 Myerson root-of-unity paper was not inspected in full; the root-sum triangle geometry is treated as prior mathematical knowledge, not novelty.
A specialized earlier Gabor-window design or unpublished identical formula could exist outside the searched published-finding corpus records and inspected primary literature.

value.rationale: Three modulation channels form the smallest nontrivial frequency-subset design in the coprime two-tap all-translation Gabor family, and spectral condition number directly measures worst-case stable reconstruction. Unlike the known balanced-root triangle or structural Fourier diagonalization, the result sharply optimizes the spectral ratio over every three-channel selection, classifies every optimum and exact tightness threshold, and shows how parity affects finite-N conditioning. The full arithmetic optimum and near-tight 1/N law give a natural reconstruction design benchmark rather than an arbitrary finite sample.
